questions.signal: Has operated a model in production and learned from it going wrong
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time a model you shipped behaved worse in production than in evaluation.
idealAnswerPoints: how the problem was detected, and whether a user or a metric found it first
the size of the gap between offline and production performance
a root cause such as drift, train/serve skew or leakage, confirmed with evidence
the specific fix they drove
the monitoring or eval change they added afterward
weakAnswerSigns: only discusses offline metrics
no root cause found
'the team' fixed it
followUpHooks: How did you first find out?
How big was the gap?
How did you separate a data problem from a model problem?
What was the actual root cause?
What monitoring did you add afterward?
Would that monitoring have caught it a week earlier?

criteria.structure: Moves from detection through diagnosis and fix to the prevention added afterward
criteria.specificity: Names the model, the metric, the size of the gap and the actual root cause
criteria.impact: States how production performance recovered, with a number
criteria.ownership: Names the debugging steps and fixes they personally drove

questions.signal: Has the engineering judgment to say a model isn't worth it, and backs it with a baseline
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you argued against using an ML model or an LLM for a problem.
idealAnswerPoints: the problem and who wanted a model for it
why a simpler approach (rules, search, a heuristic) was enough: data, accuracy needs, cost, explainability
evidence: a baseline they built, or a cost and accuracy comparison
the outcome, and whether the simpler approach held up over time
weakAnswerSigns: the objection was opinion with no baseline
the story is really about choosing one model over another
no outcome
followUpHooks: Who wanted to use a model?
What simpler approach did you propose?
How did you show it was good enough?
What would have made a model worth it?
How has the simpler approach held up since?

criteria.structure: Sets up the proposal, their counter-case, the evidence and the decision in order
criteria.specificity: Names the problem, the baseline built and the numbers compared
criteria.impact: States what was shipped and how it performed afterward
criteria.ownership: Shows they personally built the baseline and made the argument

questions.signal: Treats evaluation as the launch gate and can defend a delay with a specific flaw
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you held back a model or prompt change from launching because you didn't trust the evaluation.
idealAnswerPoints: what looked good on paper and the specific reason to doubt it: leakage, an unrepresentative eval set, judge bias, a tiny sample
what they did to get a trustworthy signal: a new eval slice, human review, shadow traffic
how they handled pressure to ship
what the better evaluation showed and the final decision
weakAnswerSigns: a gut feeling with no specific flaw in the eval
a delay with no plan to resolve it
no outcome
followUpHooks: What did the original numbers say?
What specifically made you distrust them?
Who wanted to ship anyway?
What did you do to get a number you trusted?
What did it show?
How did you change the eval process afterward?

criteria.structure: Moves from the promising result through the doubt and the better eval to the decision
criteria.specificity: Names the metric, the specific flaw in the eval and what the new eval measured
criteria.impact: States what the better eval revealed and what was shipped or stopped
criteria.ownership: Shows they personally raised the concern and built the better evaluation

questions.signal: Explains model behaviour honestly to people who don't think in probabilities
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you had to explain to a non-technical stakeholder why a model got something wrong.
idealAnswerPoints: the specific failure and the stakeholder's concern
how they explained it without jargon: concrete examples, error rates in plain terms
honest about what could and couldn't be fixed
the concrete next step agreed: a fix, a guardrail, human review or changed expectations
weakAnswerSigns: blames the stakeholder for not understanding AI
overpromises a fix
the explanation is full of jargon
followUpHooks: What exactly went wrong?
What did they think had happened?
How did you actually explain it?

Did it happen again?

criteria.structure: Sets up the failure, the conversation and the agreed next step in order
criteria.specificity: Names the failure case and how they described it in plain words
criteria.impact: States what changed afterward for the stakeholder or the product
criteria.ownership: Shows they personally owned the explanation and the follow-up

questions.signal: Traces model problems back to data and builds checks so they can't recur silently
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time bad data caused a problem in a model or pipeline you worked on.
idealAnswerPoints: the symptom and how it surfaced
how they traced it to the data: a schema change, nulls, duplicates, label errors or an upstream bug
the fix to the data and to the damage already done (retraining, backfill)
validation added at the pipeline boundary: schema, distribution or row-count checks
weakAnswerSigns: 'the data was bad' with no specific defect
fixed the data once with no check added
someone else found and fixed it

How did you trace it back to the data?
What exactly was wrong with it?
How much had it already affected?
What check did you add so it can't happen silently again?

criteria.structure: Walks from the symptom to the data defect, the fix and the prevention
criteria.specificity: Names the dataset, the specific defect and the check that was added
criteria.impact: States the damage done and what the fix recovered
criteria.ownership: Shows they personally traced and fixed it

questions.signal: Optimises against a measured baseline while proving quality held
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you cut the cost or latency of a model running in production.

the levers tried: a smaller or distilled model, caching, batching, quantisation, shorter prompts, routing
how they showed quality didn't drop, offline and online
the measured saving

criteria.structure: Moves from the baseline through what was tried to the measured result
criteria.specificity: Gives the cost or latency numbers and the specific technique used
criteria.impact: States the saving and the quality evidence side by side
criteria.ownership: Shows they personally ran the experiments and made the call

questions.signal: Runs experiments honestly and learns from negative results
questions.prompt: Tell me about a modeling idea you were confident in that didn't work.
idealAnswerPoints: the hypothesis and why they believed it
how they tested it: the baseline, the metric and the eval set
the result, stated plainly
their analysis of why it failed
what they did next with that knowledge
weakAnswerSigns: blames data or compute with no analysis
no baseline comparison
'it didn't work' with no lesson
followUpHooks: Why were you confident?
What did you compare it against?
How did you know it really didn't work, rather than being noise?
Why do you think it failed?
How long did you keep trying before stopping?
What did you do next?

criteria.specificity: Names the idea, the baseline, the metric and the result
criteria.impact: States the effect the failed experiment had on the project's direction
criteria.ownership: Shows the idea and the decision to stop were theirs

questions.signal: Gets unblocked by building the data an ML problem needs, and treats label quality as engineering
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you had to build a labelled dataset yourself because the one you needed didn't exist.
idealAnswerPoints: why no usable data existed and what the model or eval needed it for
how they decided what to label: sampling from real traffic, covering hard and rare cases
labelling guidelines and how they checked consistency, such as double-labelling a sample and measuring agreement
how many examples, how long it took and what it cost
what the dataset unlocked, and what they'd label differently now
weakAnswerSigns: labelled whatever was easiest to get with no sampling plan
no check on label quality or agreement
can't say how big the dataset was or what it was used for
followUpHooks: What did you need the data for?
How did you choose which examples to label?
How did you know the labels were consistent?
Where did labellers disagree most?
What did the dataset let you do that you couldn't before?
What would you label differently now?

criteria.structure: Moves from the missing data through how it was built to what it enabled
criteria.specificity: Names the task, the sampling approach, the dataset size and the agreement check
criteria.impact: States the model or eval result the dataset made possible
criteria.ownership: Shows they personally designed the labelling and checked its quality

questions.signal: Knows the gap between a working demo and a dependable AI product
questions.prompt: Tell me about an LLM or ML prototype you took from a demo to something real users relied on.
idealAnswerPoints: what the demo did and what broke once real users arrived
an eval set built from real usage rather than the demo examples
reliability work: fallbacks, timeouts, guardrails, validated structured output
cost and latency at real volume
monitoring and a feedback loop after launch
weakAnswerSigns: 'we deployed it' with no reliability work
the eval set is the demo examples
no data from after launch
followUpHooks: What broke first when real users touched it?
How did you evaluate it before launch?
What happens when the model call fails?
What did it cost per request at real volume?
How do you find out it's getting worse?

criteria.structure: Moves from demo through hardening and launch to how it ran afterward
criteria.specificity: Names the product, the failure modes found and the specific reliability work
criteria.impact: States usage, reliability or quality numbers after launch
criteria.ownership: Shows which hardening decisions they personally made

questions.signal: Settles modeling disagreements with experiments, not opinions
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate about which modeling approach to use.
idealAnswerPoints: both approaches stated fairly, including the merit of the other side
an experiment or comparison designed to decide it, with an agreed metric
what the result showed and the decision taken
how the working relationship held up
weakAnswerSigns: decided by seniority or volume
no experiment or shared metric
the teammate is painted as simply wrong
followUpHooks: What was their approach?
What was the strongest argument for it?
How did you decide between them?
What did the comparison show?
Who turned out to be right?

criteria.structure: Explains the two approaches, how it was decided and the result in order
criteria.specificity: Names the models or methods, the metric and the result of the comparison
criteria.impact: States what was shipped and how it performed
criteria.ownership: Describes what they personally did to settle it

questions.signal: Understands why retrieval-augmented systems fail and how to measure them
questions.prompt: Your RAG chatbot over internal docs keeps giving confident but wrong answers — how would you find out why?
idealAnswerPoints: separates retrieval failures from generation failures by inspecting the retrieved chunks for failing questions
builds a labelled set of real questions with the passages that answer them and measures retrieval recall at k
retrieval fixes tied to failure modes: chunking, hybrid keyword plus dense search, reranking, metadata filters
generation fixes: grounding instructions, citations and abstaining when the context doesn't answer
changes one thing at a time and re-runs the eval
weakAnswerSigns: only suggests a bigger model
no evaluation plan
changes several things at once without measuring
followUpHooks: How would you tell a retrieval failure from a generation failure?
How would you build an evaluation set for this?
The right chunk is retrieved but the answer is still wrong — what next?
What should it do when nothing relevant comes back?
Two documents contradict each other — which one wins?
How would you catch a regression after the next re-index?

criteria.correctness: Separates retrieval from generation and targets the stage that is actually failing
criteria.depth: Explains why each fix addresses a specific failure mode and measures it with recall or faithfulness
criteria.edge_cases: Considers empty retrieval, stale or conflicting chunks, and questions whose answer lies outside the retrieved context
criteria.communication: Explains clearly how they would isolate retrieval failures from generation failures

questions.signal: Debugs agent behaviour from traces instead of blindly editing the prompt
questions.prompt: Your tool-using agent sometimes calls the same tool over and over until it hits the step limit — how would you fix it?
idealAnswerPoints: reads traces of looping runs to see what the tool returned and what the model did next
common causes: tool errors or empty results the model can't interpret, ambiguous tool descriptions, no clear stopping condition
fixes: informative tool results and error messages, tool descriptions that say when to use them, explicit completion criteria
runtime guards: detect repeated identical calls, step and cost budgets, a graceful exit with a partial answer or escalation
a regression set of looping cases plus normal tasks to measure the fix
weakAnswerSigns: just raises the step limit
only edits the system prompt, with no traces looked at
no way to measure whether the fix worked
followUpHooks: What would you look at first?
What did the tool return on the turns where it looped?
How would you detect a loop at runtime?
What should the agent do when it gives up?
How would you know your fix didn't break other tasks?

criteria.correctness: Finds the cause in the traces and fixes it rather than raising the limit
criteria.depth: Explains why the model repeats itself given what the tool returns
criteria.edge_cases: Covers tool errors, empty results, ambiguous tools and graceful exit
criteria.communication: Describes the debugging process step by step

questions.signal: Understands indirect prompt injection and designs trust boundaries rather than trusting the prompt
questions.prompt: Your assistant reads users' incoming email and can send replies — how would you stop a malicious email from taking control of it?
idealAnswerPoints: names indirect prompt injection: untrusted content in the context can carry instructions
prompt-level defences (delimiting untrusted text, instructions) help but are not sufficient
least privilege: limit what tools can do and require user confirmation for sending or forwarding
separates reading untrusted content from taking actions, or drops tool access while untrusted content is in context
a red-team set of injection emails as a regression test, plus logging of every tool call
weakAnswerSigns: 'tell the model to ignore instructions in emails' is the whole answer
relies on an injection classifier alone
no human confirmation for high-risk actions
followUpHooks: How exactly would the attack work?
Why isn't an instruction in the system prompt enough?
Which actions would you make the user confirm?
What if the injection is hidden in an attachment or a linked page?
How would you test your defences?

criteria.correctness: Identifies indirect injection and limits what a hijacked model can do
criteria.depth: Explains why prompt-only defences fail and why privilege separation works
criteria.edge_cases: Covers hidden instructions in attachments and links, and data exfiltration through replies
criteria.communication: Explains the attack and the defence layers clearly

questions.signal: Picks metrics that match the problem instead of the default
questions.prompt: Your fraud model reports ninety-nine percent accuracy but the fraud team says it's useless — what's going on?
idealAnswerPoints: class imbalance: predicting 'not fraud' for everything scores high accuracy
precision, recall and PR-AUC instead of accuracy, noting ROC-AUC can also flatter a model under heavy imbalance
the threshold set from the cost of missed fraud versus investigator capacity
class weights or resampling, noting they distort predicted probabilities unless recalibrated
weakAnswerSigns: suggests more data or a bigger model
never mentions the base rate
switches to ROC-AUC as if that solves it
followUpHooks: What would you check first?
What would a model that never predicts fraud score?
Which metric would you use instead?
How would you pick the decision threshold?
What happens to the predicted probabilities if you oversample fraud?
Fraud labels arrive weeks later — how does that affect evaluation?

criteria.correctness: Identifies imbalance as the reason accuracy misleads
criteria.depth: Explains why precision and recall reflect the business problem and how the threshold trades them
criteria.edge_cases: Covers threshold choice, calibration after resampling and delayed labels
criteria.communication: Explains the metrics in terms the fraud team would follow

questions.signal: Understands why offline metrics and online outcomes diverge
questions.prompt: Your new ranking model beats the old one offline, but the A/B test shows no improvement — what could explain that?
idealAnswerPoints: the offline metric doesn't track the product metric
offline data was logged under the old model, so it's biased by what that model chose to show
train/serve skew: features differ between training and serving
the test itself: underpowered, diluted, novelty effects or the wrong randomisation unit
how to investigate: feature parity checks, segment results, offline-online correlation from past launches
weakAnswerSigns: concludes the test is broken without checking
suggests training longer
no mention of bias in logged data
followUpHooks: What exactly did you measure offline?
How was the offline test data collected?
How would you check the model sees the same features online?
Was the test powered to detect the gain you expected?
How would you change your offline eval so this happens less?

criteria.correctness: Names plausible causes on both the offline and online side
criteria.depth: Explains logged-data bias and metric mismatch mechanistically
criteria.edge_cases: Covers skew, underpowered tests and segment effects that cancel out
criteria.communication: Lays out an investigation order rather than a list of guesses

questions.signal: Recognises overfitting and knows the practical levers
questions.prompt: Your training loss keeps falling but your validation loss started rising a few epochs ago — what would you do?
idealAnswerPoints: identifies overfitting: the model is memorising training data
early stopping on the validation curve, keeping the best checkpoint
regularisation options: weight decay, dropout, augmentation, a smaller model
more data if available, using a learning curve to judge whether it would help
checks the validation set is representative and not leaking
weakAnswerSigns: keeps training and hopes it recovers
changes the learning rate with no reason
no idea what early stopping is
followUpHooks: What would you check first?
What's happening to the model?
Which fix would you try first?
How would you tell whether more data would help?
When would rising validation loss not mean overfitting?

criteria.correctness: Identifies overfitting and proposes a sensible first fix
criteria.depth: Explains why each lever reduces variance
criteria.edge_cases: Considers a small or unrepresentative validation set and distribution mismatch

questions.signal: Understands train/serve skew and how feature pipelines prevent it
questions.prompt: A feature is computed by a nightly batch job for training but by application code at serving time — what can go wrong?
idealAnswerPoints: the two implementations drift: null handling, units, time zones, library versions
point-in-time correctness: training must use values as they were at prediction time, or future data leaks in
freshness differs: nightly values can be a day stale at serving
one shared feature definition for both paths, such as a feature store or shared library, or logging served features for training
detection: compare served feature distributions with training distributions
weakAnswerSigns: says nothing goes wrong if the code is tested
no mention of leaking future data
no plan to detect it
followUpHooks: What's a concrete way the two values could end up different?
How would you notice it happening?
What does point-in-time correctness mean here?
How would you make both paths use the same logic?
What if serving can't afford the batch job's computation?

criteria.correctness: Identifies skew and leakage as the two core risks
criteria.depth: Explains how skew silently degrades the model and how a shared definition prevents it
criteria.edge_cases: Covers staleness, nulls, time zones and expensive features that can't run online
criteria.communication: Uses a concrete example to explain the risk

questions.signal: Designs evaluation splits that don't leak
questions.prompt: How would you split a dataset of user sessions into training and test sets for a model that predicts a user's next action?
idealAnswerPoints: a random row split leaks: the same user's sessions land in both sets
group by user so test users are unseen, when generalising to new users matters
a time-based split so the test period comes strictly after training, matching how the model is used
a validation set for tuning, separate from the final test set
checks that segments and label balance are similar across splits
weakAnswerSigns: random split with no leakage discussion
tunes on the test set
ignores time
followUpHooks: What goes wrong with a random split?
Would you split by user or by time?
Where does hyperparameter tuning happen?
Your test score is much higher than production — what would you suspect first?
How would you check the split is representative?

criteria.correctness: Produces a split that measures performance the way the model will be used
criteria.depth: Explains why user overlap and time ordering inflate scores
criteria.edge_cases: Covers tuning leakage, users with very few sessions and seasonality
criteria.communication: Explains the trade-off between user and time splits clearly

questions.signal: Knows where inference memory goes and the levers that control it
questions.prompt: Your self-hosted LLM server runs out of GPU memory as soon as a few long conversations run at once — what's using the memory?
idealAnswerPoints: weights are fixed, but the KV cache grows with sequence length times the number of concurrent requests
a rough per-token estimate: layers times key and value heads times head size times bytes per value
fixes: paged KV cache allocation to avoid fragmentation, caps on context length or concurrency, KV cache quantisation
model-side options: grouped-query attention, weight quantisation to free memory for the cache
the trade-offs between throughput, latency and maximum context, and admission control
weakAnswerSigns: just buy bigger GPUs
thinks the weights grow with the number of users
doesn't know the KV cache exists
followUpHooks: What would you look at first?
What's stored in GPU memory besides the weights?
How does that grow with conversation length?
Roughly how would you estimate it per token?
How would you fit more concurrent users on the same GPU?
What do you give up with each of those options?

criteria.correctness: Identifies the KV cache as the memory that grows with load
criteria.depth: Explains why it scales with tokens and concurrency and how to estimate it
criteria.edge_cases: Covers fragmentation, very long contexts and bursts of concurrent requests

questions.source: adapted from KalyanKS LLM Interview Questions and Answers Hub

questions.signal: Applies statistics to a real launch decision
questions.prompt: An A/B test of your new recommendation model shows a two percent lift after three days — would you ship it?
idealAnswerPoints: looks at the confidence interval and significance, not just the point estimate
asks whether sample size was planned for this effect size, or whether this is early peeking
novelty effects and weekly cycles make three days short
checks guardrail metrics (latency, complaints, revenue) and segment effects
checks randomisation health, such as a sample ratio mismatch
weakAnswerSigns: ships because the number is positive
never asks about variance
stops the test the first time it looks significant
followUpHooks: What would you need to know about that two percent?
What's wrong with checking every day and stopping when it looks significant?
Why might three days be misleading?
What other metrics would you check before shipping?
How would you notice the randomisation was broken?

criteria.correctness: Reaches a defensible ship decision based on uncertainty, not the point estimate
criteria.depth: Explains why peeking inflates false positives and how power relates to effect size
criteria.edge_cases: Covers novelty, weekly cycles, guardrails and sample ratio mismatch
criteria.communication: Explains the statistics in plain terms

questions.signal: Knows embeddings from different models aren't comparable and can write a safe, resumable migration
questions.prompt: How would you write the job that re-embeds your document corpus when you switch to a new embedding model?
idealAnswerPoints: vectors from two models live in different spaces even at the same dimension, so old and new can never share an index or be compared
builds a new index alongside the old one, keeps serving from the old, and writes new or edited documents to both during the backfill
stores model name and version plus a content hash with each vector, so reruns skip unchanged documents and only changed ones are re-embedded
batched, rate-limited, checkpointed backfill with idempotent upserts so a crash resumes instead of restarting
compares retrieval recall on a labelled query set before cutting over, and keeps the old index for rollback
re-embeds queries with the same new model at cutover, since query and document vectors must match
weakAnswerSigns: overwrites vectors in place in the live index
assumes vectors with the same dimension are interchangeable
no evaluation before switching traffic
re-embeds everything from scratch on every run
followUpHooks: Why can't you just overwrite the vectors in place?
What if the new model has the same dimension as the old one?
How does the job know which documents still need embedding?
What happens to documents edited while the backfill is running?
How would you decide it's safe to switch queries to the new index?
The job dies halfway through — what happens?

criteria.correctness: Never mixes vectors from two models and switches queries and documents together
criteria.depth: Explains why embedding spaces are incompatible and how versioning and hashing make the job incremental
criteria.edge_cases: Covers edits during backfill, crashes mid-run, rate limits and rollback
criteria.communication: Describes the job's stages in a clear order

questions.signal: Connects vector maths to efficient code and knows when to reach for an index
questions.prompt: How would you find the documents most similar to a query among a million embeddings in Python?
idealAnswerPoints: normalises vectors so cosine similarity becomes a dot product
one matrix-vector product in numpy, then argpartition for the top k instead of a full sort
a memory estimate: count times dimension times bytes per value
for many queries or a much larger corpus, an approximate index (HNSW, IVF) and its recall trade-off
weakAnswerSigns: a Python loop over every vector
sorts all the scores
uses an approximate index without knowing it's approximate
followUpHooks: Which similarity measure would you use?
How would you avoid a Python loop?
How much memory do the embeddings take?
Why not just sort all the scores?
When would you switch to an approximate index?
How would you measure the recall you lose with it?

criteria.correctness: Returns the true top-k by cosine similarity
criteria.depth: Explains why normalisation turns cosine into a dot product and the cost of top-k selection
criteria.edge_cases: Covers memory limits, many concurrent queries and the recall of approximate search
criteria.communication: Explains the maths and the code path clearly

questions.signal: Designs a RAG system end to end, including permissions, freshness and evaluation
questions.prompt: Design an assistant that answers employees' questions using the company's internal documents.
idealAnswerPoints: clarifies document sources, permissions, how fresh answers must be and what a good answer is
ingestion: parsing, chunking, embeddings and incremental re-indexing on edits and deletes
permission-aware retrieval that filters by the asking user's access at query time
hybrid retrieval plus reranking, answers with citations, and abstaining when context is insufficient
an eval set of real questions with expected sources, measuring retrieval recall and answer faithfulness
cost and latency per query, monitoring and user feedback capture
weakAnswerSigns: embeds everything with no permission model
no evaluation plan
no plan for documents changing
followUpHooks: What would you want to know before you start designing?
How do documents get into the system?
How do you stop someone getting an answer from a document they can't access?
How do you know the answers are good?
A document is edited — how long until answers reflect it?
Where would you spend money to make it better, retrieval or the model?

criteria.requirements: Clarifies sources, permissions, freshness and what a good answer means before designing
criteria.scalability: Explains how ingestion and retrieval scale with corpus size and query volume, and what each query costs
criteria.tradeoffs: Weighs chunking, retrieval and model choices against cost and quality
criteria.depth: Goes deep on permission-aware retrieval, re-indexing or the evaluation plan

questions.signal: Treats evaluation as infrastructure: representative data, calibrated scoring and release gates
questions.prompt: Design the system that decides whether a new prompt or model version is good enough to ship.
idealAnswerPoints: clarifies the product tasks, the cost of each failure type and who signs off
versioned golden sets per task built from real traffic, including hard and safety cases
scoring: programmatic checks where possible, an LLM judge calibrated against human labels, a human review sample
regression gates in CI comparing against the current version, with enough examples to trust the difference
an online stage: shadow or canary traffic with product metrics and guardrails
eval sets kept fresh by adding production failures
weakAnswerSigns: eyeballs a handful of examples
an LLM judge with no calibration
no online stage
followUpHooks: What questions do you have before we start?
Where do your test cases come from?
How do you score open-ended answers?
How do you know the LLM judge agrees with people?
The new version is better on average but worse on one category — do you ship?
How do you stop the eval set going stale?

criteria.requirements: Defines what good enough means per task and who decides before designing the pipeline
criteria.scalability: Explains how eval cost and time scale with the number of cases, versions and judges
criteria.tradeoffs: Weighs programmatic, LLM-judge and human scoring on cost and trustworthiness
criteria.depth: Goes deep on judge calibration, release gates or keeping eval sets representative

questions.signal: Understands LLM inference economics: batching, memory, GPU utilisation and latency targets
questions.prompt: Design a platform that serves open-weight LLMs to teams across the company.
idealAnswerPoints: clarifies models, traffic shape, latency targets (time to first token versus throughput) and interactive versus batch use
an inference engine with continuous batching and paged KV cache
GPU capacity: model placement, tensor parallelism for large models, autoscaling with slow model loads
routing, per-team quotas and priority between interactive and batch traffic
quantisation and speculative decoding as cost and latency levers
metrics: time to first token, tokens per second, GPU utilisation, queue depth, cost per token
weakAnswerSigns: one request per GPU at a time with no batching
autoscales as if model servers were stateless web servers that start instantly
no distinction between latency and throughput
followUpHooks: What would you want to know before you start designing?
How do you get good GPU utilisation?
A model takes minutes to load — how does that change autoscaling?
How do you stop a batch job starving interactive users?
Where does most of the cost go?
What breaks first when traffic doubles?

criteria.requirements: Clarifies models, traffic mix and which latency metric matters before designing
criteria.scalability: Explains how batching, placement and autoscaling determine GPU utilisation and capacity
criteria.tradeoffs: Weighs latency against throughput and cost, including quantisation's quality cost
criteria.depth: Goes deep on batching and KV cache memory, scheduling or autoscaling

questions.signal: Designs shared LLM infrastructure with quotas, fallback, cost attribution and data controls
questions.prompt: Design a gateway that every team in the company uses to call external LLM providers.
idealAnswerPoints: clarifies providers, how many teams, cost-tracking needs and data policy
one API across providers, with routing and fallback when a provider errors or slows down
per-team keys, quotas, rate limits and cost attribution
caching: exact-match, and semantic caching with its wrong-hit risk
PII redaction or policy enforcement, and logging with retention controls
streaming support and the gateway's own added latency
weakAnswerSigns: a thin proxy with no quotas or cost tracking
fails over blindly between models that behave differently
semantic caching with no thought about wrong hits
followUpHooks: What questions do you have before we start?
What does the API look like to a calling team?
A provider starts timing out — what happens to requests?
How do you attribute cost to teams?
When is caching responses dangerous?
